newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans, heating oil prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans, heating oil prices fall.

text.p: Soybean prices tumbled Wednesday on signs that export sales could be slowing and heating oil prices fell after data showed stockpiles growing.
November soybeans fell nine cents to $6.89-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade after almost 2 million bushels of soybeans were registered as eligible for delivery during the session.
The move was a strong sign that recent booming soybean exports could be cooling off, traders said.
"That's what broke the market, that and local selling. There should be two to three million beans tomorrow for delivery," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
The Department of Agriculture this month estimated the domestic crop at 2.35 billion bushels, which would be second biggest ever, and traders said that estimate could rise next month.
Meanwhile, weekly export data for soybeans, due on Thursday, were expected to show a decline from the strong 1.4 million metric tons reported sold a week ago.
"There's certainly not the business this week we saw last week," said analyst Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
The selling in soybeans, a favourite of professional speculators and funds, carried over to corn.
December corn fell 4-1/4 cents to $2.70-1/4 a bushel at the CBOT, with prospects of a larger crop somewhat offset by slow sales by farmers of newly harvested crop to grain elevators.
Heating oil fell sharply and gasoline prices rose after weekly statistics on stockpiles released late on Tuesday. Crude prices ended little changed.

November heating oil fell 1.37 cents to 68.46 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. November unleaded gasoline rose 0.90 cent to 70 cents a gallon and December crude oil fell 6 cents to $24.28 a barrel.

"The factors that pulled heating oil and crude up, like Middle East tensions -- specifically in Iraq -- and low heating oil stocks, are now losing their steam," said Paul Ting, senior oil and gas analyst with Salomon Brothers.

The American Petroleum Institute said stocks of heating oil and other distillates grew 3.6 million barrels in the week ended Oct. 25, a bigger buildup than the 1 million- to 3 million-barrel rise traders had expected.
"We have started to turn the corner into a market downtrend," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co.

Crude stocks fell 2.5 million barrels compared with an expected drop of up to 2 million barrels. Gasoline stocks fell 3.8 million barrels, a sharper drop than the expected decline of up to 3 million barrels.
Oil prices had jumped 30 percent and heating oil 50 percent since mid-summer to last week's post-Gulf War highs, spurred mainly by low stockpiles of heating oil and diesel fuel.

Two weeks ago, Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary met with oil executives to discuss the low heating oil stocks, but analysts said refineries had already stepped up output to take advantage of the higher prices.
"O'Leary did what she had to do, but there was never a question that refiners had already started to maximize heat production," said Bruce Lanni, Oppenheimer & Co. oil analyst.
Elsewhere, lumber futures fell the $10 daily limit on signs recent strong demand was easing. The November contract ended at $412.20 for 1,000 board feet at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
